title: No Application Fee Universities in Europe 2027: Where Applying Costs Nothing
seoTitle: No Application Fee Universities Europe 2027: Free Countries List
seoDescription: Which European universities charge no application fee in 2027: Norway, Denmark, Germany, Italy and more — plus a 10-application portfolio that costs under €200.
intro: Most of continental Europe charges nothing to apply. Where the fee-free systems are, and how to build a funded 10-application portfolio for under €200.
description: European universities without application fees in 2027: country-by-country costs and a sub-€200 application strategy.
author: NextApply Team
excerpt: Where European applications are free — and how to build a 10-application portfolio for under €200.
content:
Application fees are a quiet tax on ambitious students. Apply to ten universities across the UK and the Netherlands and you can spend €1,200 before writing a single motivation letter. Yet most of continental Europe charges nothing at all — and knowing where the fee-free systems sit changes how many applications a modest budget can carry. This guide maps the landscape for the 2027 intake and shows how to build a ten-application portfolio for under €200.

Where applications are genuinely free

Country / systemApplication cost for non-EU applicants
NorwayFree — no application fee at public universities
DenmarkFree — doctoral and master’s applications carry no fee
Germany (direct)Free at most universities that run their own portals
Germany (uni-assist)€75 for the first application, €30 for each additional one
ItalyFree or nominal (€0-30) at most public universities
AustriaOften free for degree applications; €75-100 in some cases
Erasmus Mundus programmesMostly free; a minority charge €30-50
SwitzerlandCHF 50-150 per institution
FranceCampus France processing fee (about €100) covers the procedure
SwedenSEK 900 (about €80) — one fee covers all applications in a round
NetherlandsAbout €100 for non-EU applicants at most universities

The pattern is consistent: countries that treat admission as a public service — Norway, Denmark, most of Germany and Italy — charge nothing, while systems with individual assessment (the Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland) charge a processing fee that rarely exceeds €100. Doctoral applications are free nearly everywhere in Europe; fees concentrate at master’s level.

[[chart:appfees]]

The ten-application, sub-€200 portfolio

Here is what a realistic funded-application season looks like when fees are engineered out:

  • 3 Erasmus Mundus programmes — free at most consortia, and the rules let you hold scholarship applications at three. Our deadline calendar picks the months.
  • 3 German universities or IMPRS programmes — free directly, or €105 total through uni-assist if your targets use it.
  • 2 Nordic positions — free in Norway and Denmark; Sweden’s single SEK 900 fee covers every university in one round.
  • 2 Italian programmes — free or nominal, with the DSU grant application free as well.

Total: €0-190, with eleven funded doors open. The same portfolio aimed at UK (£application fees — where they exist — of £25-90 each) and Dutch universities doubles the cost before travel or tests.

Where the money actually goes

Budget honesty: the fee is the smallest line item. English tests (€200-250), transcript apostilles and translations (€50-300 depending on country), and passports dominate. Prioritise accordingly — a single IELTS sitting costs more than every application fee in the portfolio above, which is why our without-IELTS strategies save real money rather than symbolise it. Fee-free systems also tend to be documentary-strict: free to apply does not mean easy to win, and eligibility screens reject incomplete files without a refund because there was nothing to refund.

The fees that replace application fees

Fee-free admission does not mean fee-free enrolment, and the second fee schedule is the one that catches budgets. German universities charge semester contributions of €150-350 — a social ticket covering transport, not tuition, but payable before you can register. Residence permits cost €75-114 in Germany, €228-243 in the Netherlands, and more with dependants. Visa application fees run €75-100 nearly everywhere. France’s Campus France processing fee and Italy’s occasional €30 programme fees play the same role at the front door. Budget these enrolment-stage costs now, because they all fall due in the same six weeks — offer accepted, permit filed, registration paid — and none of them are refundable.

One more line belongs in every fee-planning table: scholarship applications themselves. Every major scheme in our guides — Erasmus Mundus, Türkiye Bursları, Stipendium Hungaricum, the Government of Ireland awards, DAAD — applies for free. Anyone charging you to submit a scholarship application is not part of the process.

What free application fees do NOT mean

Three misconceptions cost applicants real money every year. Free application is not free enrolment — Sweden’s tuition for non-EU students is substantial despite the modest SEK 900 fee; Norway is the true tuition-free outlier. Free does not mean unconditional — German universities still demand APS certificates from some countries and recognised degrees everywhere. And “no fee” never describes agents’ charges — every system above is designed to be applied to directly, free, by the applicant. The funded positions below — Nordic, German, Italian — all sit in fee-free or near-free systems, and every one of them pays you rather than the reverse.
